title: Erie, the Cat Nation
summary: The Erie were an Iroquoian people whose homeland lay south of Lake Erie. The Haudenosaunee dispersed them around 1654–57.
bodyMarkdown:
The Erie were an Iroquoian-speaking people who lived south of Lake Erie until the mid-1600s. The French called them la Nation du Chat, the Cat Nation. They never lived in Kentucky, but their defeat was part of the wars that shaped later claims to the Ohio Valley.

## Name and homeland

The [Wikipedia article on the Erie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erie_people) lists their names as Erie, Eriehronon, Ehriehronnons and la Nation du Chat. It says "cat" may have meant the raccoon, since settlers in New France called raccoons chats sauvages. [Grokipedia's Erie article](https://grokipedia.com/page/Erie_people) translates the Iroquoian name as "long tail" or "people of the long tail," pointing to the raccoon or possibly the eastern panther. It adds that Lake Erie took its name from them in French usage around 1640.

Grokipedia places their territory along the south shore of Lake Erie, across parts of today's northern Ohio, northwestern Pennsylvania and western New York. Like their Wendat (Huron), Neutral and Seneca neighbors, they lived in bark longhouses inside palisaded villages and grew crops. Grokipedia also describes them as skilled tobacco growers and traders.

## War with the Haudenosaunee

From about 1640 the Haudenosaunee, or Five Nations Iroquois, fought a long series of conflicts with their neighbors that historians call the [Beaver Wars](/stories/iroquois-beaver-wars/). [Grokipedia's Beaver Wars article](https://grokipedia.com/page/Beaver_Wars) says overhunting had stripped beaver from Haudenosaunee lands. The confederacy then turned on rival peoples, including the Huron, Neutral and Erie, to gain hunting grounds and control of the fur trade.

Tensions with the Erie built through the early 1650s. Wikipedia says that in May 1654 the Onondaga told the French they would lead an army against the Erie that summer. A force of about 1,200 Onondaga and Seneca warriors, many with Dutch muskets, besieged an Erie fort. The Erie had fired arrows so fast that the attackers used their canoes as shields and as ladders to climb the palisade.

By 1656, Wikipedia says, the Erie confederacy no longer existed. Many captives, mostly women and children, were adopted into Onondaga and Seneca communities. Some historians link Erie refugees to the Richahecrians, who appeared in Virginia in 1656, and to the later Westo of the Savannah River.

## Why they matter to Kentucky

Grokipedia notes that by the 1670s the Five Nations claimed the Ohio Country as their hunting ground. That claim mattered a century later, when the Six Nations ceded Kentucky lands to the British Crown in the [Treaty of Fort Stanwix](/stories/treaty-of-fort-stanwix-1768/). The [Wikipedia article on the Beaver Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beaver_Wars) says the Shawnee and Miami were the dominant peoples of the Ohio Country, and that Haudenosaunee attacks forced the Shawnee out of their holdings in central Ohio. Later Shawnee life on the Ohio is told in [Lower Shawneetown](/stories/lower-shawneetown-at-the-scioto-mouth/).

## Kentucky today

No Erie community survives under that name. Wikipedia says Erie descendants live on among Haudenosaunee communities in New York, Oklahoma and Ontario. The Erie appear in Kentucky history only through the wars and later land claims of other nations.
